 Challenging all-round workload and desire to push for Australia selection led to former NSW captain's decision to step down
 Jack Edwards says stepping back from the NSW captaincy has freed him up to realise his full potential as an allrounder as he seeks to nail down a regular spot in Australia's white-ball sides.
 Edwards has debuted in both of Australia's T20 (against Pakistan in January) and 50-over (against South Africa in September) teams this year. He's set to play his first internationals on home soil this month after being named in both squads to face England, with the ODI series to kick off in Perth on Friday.
 Australia v England, first ODI: match preview 
 The 26-year-old relinquished the Blues' Sheffield Shield and one-day leadership during the second half of last summer after just over a year at the helm, with Nic Maddinson and Lachlan Shaw appointed his successors ahead of this season .
 Edwards said his skillset as a pace-bowling allrounder combined with the state captaincy was a "very large workload".

 Former NSW skipper Edwards takes down Tassie 
 "I played a lot of cricket last year and trying to captain the four-day team was quite challenging as an allrounder," he said at Perth Stadium on Tuesday.
 "I really wanted to push my case to play cricket for Australia and keep being the best player that I could be for NSW, and I felt like the captaincy was maybe just a bit too much for me at that point.
 "(The decision to step down) has just allowed me to freshen up and focus on myself a little bit more and try to manage the mental and physical load of being an allrounder, because it's very hard work.
 "I did enjoy the captaincy, and it might be for me again down the line.
 "But for now, it's been great to see some other guys step up into the leadership roles."

 Details on new NSW skippers as Edwards shifts focus 
 After a luckless run with injuries through the early stages of his career, the right-armer's bowling workloads have drastically increased over the past four Sheffield Shield seasons, sending down an average of 26 overs per match (up from 10 overs prior).
 Since the start of the 2023-24 season, he's taken 73 wickets at an average of 25 in 26 first-class matches while also averaging 40 with the bat during the same period.
 An impressive BBL|15 with the ball for Sydney Sixers last summer (19 wickets) catapulted Edwards into the national frame to earn his T20I cap in Lahore, while he also took 4-56 and scored a 75-ball 89 during Australia A's 50-over tour of India last year.

 Five-wicket hauls, finals and more in Edwards' best year yet 
 The ODI retirement of Marcus Stoinis, captain Mitch Marsh hanging up his bowling boots, and Cameron Green's workloads being closely monitored following back surgery in late 2024 have left a void in Australia's white-ball set-up for a new pace-bowling allrounder to step into.
 "I've worked really hard to get an opportunity like this and I want to take it," Edwards, who opened the batting for Australia in the 2018 Under-19 World Cup, said of his senior call-up.
 "Knowing that what I do, the strengths and qualities that I bring can hopefully be good enough, has allowed me to be myself and go out there and compete as hard as I can and enjoy (playing international cricket).
 "It's something I've worked a long time for to be able to play for Australia and play in front of the big crowds, so I'm just trying to take it all in and be grateful for the experience.
 Cummins' quip sums up Edwards' peculiar road to ODI cap 
 "If I get the opportunity this week and down the line, then hopefully I can take it and keep trying to get better each day with both bat and ball."
 Buoyed by his five-wicket return in the second ODI against South Africa where Marsh entrusted him to bowl the tough death overs as the hosts piled on 9-365, Edwards returned from his second Australian tour with the belief he belongs there.
 "I took a lot of confidence away from it, that what I've been doing back home domestically stands up at that international level," he said.

 Edwards steps up to deliver crucial five-wicket haul 
 "It's important to me that I can bowl in all three phases of the game.
 "Domestically, coming through (at NSW and the Sixers), I've had those opportunities and those challenges of bowling at the death and with a new ball, and it was nice in South Africa to get the opportunity to showcase that.
 "Hopefully I can keep improving those areas and show that, from the bowling side of things, that I can handle it.
 "It was a tough series (Australia lost 2-1) … and it just made me hungrier to get back there and do it again."
